summary: Extends NETCONF to support the Network Management Datastore Architecture from RFC 8342. It adds get-data and edit-data operations and updates RFC 6241 and RFC 7950.

plainLanguage.summary: The device now has several kinds of settings lists. This adds new commands to read and edit each one.

questions: what is the netconf get-data operation
subtitle: New NETCONF operations and YANG library rules so clients can work with every datastore in the NMDA.

tldr.problem: The original NETCONF operations such as get-config and edit-config use a fixed choice of datastores, which does not fit a server that implements the Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA).
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds get-data and edit-data operations that name a datastore by identity, adds a datastore leaf to lock, unlock and validate, and requires NMDA servers to support the YANG library and advertise it in the hello message.
tldr.outcome: Clients can read and edit all datastores a server supports, including the operational state datastore, and discover which datastores and modules exist. It updates RFC 6241 and RFC 7950.

today: RFC 8526 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2019. It has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC, and it updates RFC 6241 and RFC 7950.

sections.title: What This RFC Changes
sections.content:
This RFC extends NETCONF from RFC 6241 to support the Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA) from RFC 8342. It lets NETCONF clients interact with all the datastores a server supports.

It updates RFC 6241 by adding the <get-data> and <edit-data> operations and by augmenting <lock>, <unlock> and <validate>. It updates RFC 7950 so that clients can discover which datastores a server supports and which modules each one has, which requires NMDA servers to support the YANG library of RFC 8525.
sections.plainLanguage: Devices now have more than one kind of settings list. The old commands only knew about the old lists, so new commands were needed.

sections.title: Server and YANG Library Requirements
sections.content:
An NMDA-compliant NETCONF server MUST implement the ietf-netconf-nmda module, MUST support the operational state datastore, and MUST implement at least revision 2019-01-04 of the ietf-yang-library module from RFC 8525. A client finds the supported datastores and modules by reading the YANG library from the operational state datastore.

The server MUST also advertise a capability in its hello message, urn:ietf:params:netconf:capability:yang-library:1.1, with a revision parameter and a content-id parameter. Both MUST be present. A client can cache the datastores and modules and refresh the cache only when the content-id value changes.

This updates Section 5.6.4 of RFC 7950, allowing servers to advertise :yang-library:1.1 instead of :yang-library:1.0 and to implement the subtree /yang-library instead of /modules-state.
sections.plainLanguage: The device must tell you in its greeting which lists it has. If the greeting number stays the same, you can reuse what you remembered.

sections.title: The get-data Operation
sections.content:
<get-data> retrieves data from a specific NMDA datastore. It is like <get-config> but lets the client pick the source datastore with the datastore parameter, which is a datastore identity. Using identities allows future expansion in a way the choice-based design of the original operations does not.

Filtering is richer. It uses an explicit subtree-filter or xpath-filter, a config-filter to get only 'config true' or 'config false' nodes, and origin-filter or negated-origin-filter, which cannot be used together. A max-depth parameter limits the subtree levels returned.

The with-origin parameter asks for origin metadata annotations, which say where operational values came from. It is valid only for the operational state datastore and datastores derived from it, and is OPTIONAL under the feature origin. The with-defaults parameter of RFC 6243 works for conventional configuration datastores when the capability is supported. For the operational datastore it is OPTIONAL and uses the capability urn:ietf:params:netconf:capability:with-operational-defaults:1.0.
sections.plainLanguage: Get-data is like asking 'show me the list called this', and you can say which list and ask for only the parts you want.

sections.title: The edit-data and Augmented Operations
sections.content:
<edit-data> changes a writable datastore, like <edit-config> but with a datastore identity naming the target. Using it on a non-writable datastore returns an error. Its default-operation parameter copies the one in <edit-config>, and edit-content is either config or url. The config element uses anydata instead of anyxml.

<edit-data> does not support the error-option and test-option parameters. Its error behavior matches the rollback-on-error value of error-option.

The existing <lock>, <unlock> and <validate> operations get a new datastore leaf. If one of them is not supported on a datastore, an error is returned.
sections.plainLanguage: Edit-data is the same idea for changing a list: you say which list to change. Lock, unlock and validate also learn to take a list name.

sections.title: Examples from the RFC
sections.content:
The RFC translates examples from RFC 6241. One <get-data> request names ds:running as the datastore and uses a subtree filter to select the entire /users subtree.

Another targets ds:operational with a subtree filter on a BGP data model, two origin-filter entries (or:intended and or:system) and with-origin. Adding config-filter set to true leaves out system state nodes such as state. An <edit-data> example sets the MTU to 1500 on interface Ethernet0/0 in ds:running and gets <ok/> back.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show asking for the 'running' list or the 'what is really happening' list, and changing one number on one interface.

sections.title: IANA and Security Considerations
sections.content:
IANA registers two NETCONF capability URNs, :yang-library:1.1 and :with-operational-defaults. It also registers the XML namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-netconf-nmda and the YANG module ietf-netconf-nmda with prefix ncds.

On security, the module extends the base NETCONF operations. The lowest NETCONF layer is the secure transport and the mandatory-to-implement transport is Secure Shell (RFC 6242). The Network Configuration Access Control Model (RFC 8341) can restrict users to a subset of operations and content. The security considerations of RFC 6241 apply to <get-data> and <edit-data>.
sections.plainLanguage: The new commands use the same locked tunnel as the old ones, and the same rules can limit who is allowed to use them.
